div.head: Chapter 16
div.p: The second part of the said seventh principle; namely, the course of government that has been imposed upon those peoples and lands, any prudent reader may come to understand what it must have been like from the proofs of fact and of law brought above for the first part.

This has been, and is, the dividing among themselves by the Spaniards of the towns of the Indians, which they called repartimientos, and afterwards, to give them a more honorable name, they called them encomiendas. In many parts of the Indies they divided out not only towns, but the very persons of a town: men, women, children and old people, assigning to one Spaniard fifty, to another a hundred, to another two hundred, according to the favor each enjoyed with the captain or governor, and greater tyrant, who distributed them. And to the one he most wished to honor and benefit he gave the natural lord or lords of the town, so that they too might serve him in the same manner as their subjects. This natural lord served like the others, and was in greater servitude, because if any of the subjects, on account of the labors and sufferings they bore, fled and failed to appear for the work and services, the wretched lord suffered for it in blows and lashes and in prison and the stocks, like the overseers of Israel who were like the foremen of the working parties, who when the daily quota fell short of the number of bricks the tyrant Pharaoh had imposed as tribute were beaten and cruelly afflicted, as appears from Exodus, chapter 5: "And the overseers of the works of the children of Israel were beaten by the taskmasters of Pharaoh, saying: why have you not fulfilled your quota of bricks as before, neither yesterday nor today? etc." Which in truth was fulfilled and is fulfilled today to the letter throughout all the Indies.

The afflictions and oppressions and harsh servitude that all those peoples have suffered and suffer, on account of the insupportable tributes and burdens that have been imposed upon them in diverse ways, cannot be believed; but in truth and with truth we affirm that it is far more than we here describe. And what with the most shameless brazenness and profound insensibility the sinful tyrants, more cruel than Pharaoh, dare to say is that the Indians are lazy and idle and can contribute more in tributes and services: the very words Pharaoh said: "You are idle, and therefore straw shall not be given to you, etc." — giving them no time or space even to breathe, and far harder than Pharaoh dealt with the Israelites.

That these repartimientos and encomiendas and this manner of governing are violent, unjust, abominable, tyrannical, and most cruel, though it is plain in itself if one looks with free and compassionate eyes: I wish nonetheless to set down only some brief and simple reasons, leaving the full proof of this to our other treatises, where it has been sufficiently and amply proved.

Let the first be this: that manner of ruling or governing free men or peoples is violent, unjust, abominable, and most cruel that deprives subjects of all their liberty, in such a way that they cannot freely dispose of their own persons or of those in their charge, such as their children and dependents. Now the said repartimientos are of this kind; therefore they are violent, tyrannical, unjust, and most cruel. The major premise is clear.

The minor is proved because, after being distributed wherever they were distributed, by persons or by heads, as in Hispaniola and the other islands, and in Nicaragua, and in Venezuela and Popayán and in Chile and in other places, all of them entirely, small and great, women and men, pregnant and newly delivered, young and old, boys and girls, lords and subjects, healthy and sick, were and are placed in such servitude to the Spaniards that not an hour did they or do they leave them to breathe without being occupied, whether in the mines or in the fields, or in carrying loads on their backs for any distance, like beasts; and when men are lacking or occupied, women serve as pack animals, carrying the loads, and in all the things they need them for, day and night, as if they were slaves bought and sold, taken in a just war; and commonly all their services are rendered by compulsion, so that not only do they perform the labors and tasks and serve as described, but all of this at their own cost and on their own food, even if they must come from twenty or fifty or more leagues away: they must bring what they are to eat on the journey there, and for the time spent on the labors and estates — digging and doing everything men and beasts must do as commanded — and then for the return journey to their lands and homes.

And the Indians of towns that are not distributed by heads, but where an entire town or towns are given to a Spaniard to serve him, together with their natural lord or lords, are in other ways harassed and oppressed and live the life of the desperate and the wretched. These are the tributes, so many and of so many kinds, that neither the living nor the dead have ever seen or heard of impositions so impossible, cruel, and execrable, upon human beings. I wish to give the example of a town in the bishopric of Chiapa of five hundred households, within which dwell husbands and wives and their young children, who must provide sixty or seventy men daily to come and work at whatever the encomendero orders them. Item, that the whole town sow a field of thirty fanegas of maize each year, and tend and weed and cultivate it until the harvest; in sowing this maize they spend a great deal of time, because they sow it grain by grain. Item, that they sow for him seven fanegas of wheat, and another six fanegas of beans, which are like lupins or broad beans, and two fanegas of cotton. Item, that he may extract from the town each year twelve hundred men — which is barely more people than the entire town possesses — to be loaded up and carry the Spaniard's goods, such as sugar or other things, to the port that lies forty leagues from the said town; and for this transport the encomendero gives each one one hundred cacao beans or almonds, worth up to twenty maravedís the hundred. Item, two hundred xequíniles of cacao, which is a measure holding eight thousand almonds, something they must grow from their own harvest, and yet must go to buy in other lands or provinces. Item, that they give sixty fanegas of salt, for which they must go to the sea, twenty or thirty leagues from their homes, either to buy it or to make it, where they spend many days. Item, that each Easter they give him fifty cotton blankets two yards square, and fifty shirts for the people of his household. These people do not grow cotton because the land is not suited to it, and they must go to buy it thirty or forty leagues away and carry it back on their shoulders, and then spin it, and then weave it, and then sew the shirts; and a people who have in their lives no more means than what they earn in daily toil to sustain themselves and their wives and children: with what shall they buy in other lands what they do not have or grow? They obtain it by going to serve for some time among the peoples who have those things; and because where they go to buy it is hot country, many die before they can return to their homes.

Item, that he give the encomendero twelve native turkeys — for they are large birds like overgrown fowl that take three or four years to mature properly — and at each Easter, seventy birds, half of those native ones, and the other thirty-five of the Castilian kind.

Item, that from all the said maize and wheat and everything else they sow and harvest, as described, they carry it to the city on their backs, as much as is needed. Item, that they provision and maintain the sugar mill and the estate with food, where there are usually a hundred and fifty persons, and works arise at the mill requiring three hundred men to gather, as was done to carry from several leagues away a great beam that had broken, and to renovate the buildings and other great labors and tasks that arise at the mills every hour. And this has no limit, but whenever the encomendero wishes or has need, they must do all of it at their own cost, beyond everything already said and yet to be said. Item, that they give him all the chacunites and petacas — which are the boxes like baskets in the shape of chests made of wicker or canes covered with deerskins — as many as he needs for his household and to pack the sugar from the mill. Item, all the planking needed to make the crates in which the sugar is to be sent to Castile. Truly, this last item alone, with no limit in number or measure, would be an intolerable tribute and burden for the city of Écija or the town of Madrid. For this task alone there are dedicated many Indian households, husbands and wives and children, who do nothing else but work at making the said vessels or baskets; and a very great number of Indians besides, searching, hunting, and killing deer to cover them with their hides. Another no small number cutting trees and sawing planks for the said crates. All of this at their own cost, and they must find their own food for themselves and for their wives and children. What greater cruelty or greater tyranny can be imagined? And yet there is more.
Item, that they bring from Tehuantepec, which is a seaport that lies a full forty leagues from their town, all the fish and shrimp needed for his household.

Item, that they give him all the Indians he needs as messengers, to send wherever he wishes. Item, that they give him each year for his household and people a hundred pairs of sandals, and fifty cotaras, which are a certain kind of footwear for the feet such as the ancients used, as appears in the tapestry hangings. Item, if he wishes to plant and establish a grove of mulberry trees to make silk, that they may plant and tend them.

Item, that they watch over all his livestock: pigs and cattle and sheep, and repair the houses and corrals of his herding stations, and his own house in the city. For the livestock he has six households of neighbors, small and great, who do nothing else.
Item, all the pitchers and pots and jars and grinding stones for maize, and other small things — the assessment says — of which his house and estate may have need.

Item, that they spin some cotton for necessary things in his household; and that each week they give him a hundred eggs; and when he is at the mill of his estate — which is like a farmstead or country property here in Spain — that they give him the fruit and food he needs; and it has happened that he took with him eighty Indians loaded with his provisions. Item, that each year they give him twenty jars of honey, which they must go seeking through the forests, and other small loads of wax; and those who drew up this assessment ordered that the Indians who serve at the mill should not work more than from sunrise to sunset.

To this I will add that to round out and justify all these tributes, the assessors of these tributes ordered that the Indians give him each year ten jaguar hides, for the taking of one of which a thousand Indians gather in the forests, and before they take and kill it it has torn apart and disemboweled fifteen or twenty Indians, for it is a most ferocious animal and very hard to overcome. This assessment for this town and its subject settlements — which are the inhabitants described — was made by a bishop and a tyrant who was rather notorious for killing Indians, that one may see the ignorance and blindness of the bishop and the wickedness of the tyrant.

And though this appears — as it is — abominable and worthy of hellfire, there are without comparison other assessments far more cruel in many parts of the Indies, especially in the provinces of Peru. I well believe it stands proved that such encomiendas and the government of the Indies are iniquitous, abominable, and tyrannical, etc.
